doc.title: Tom Baker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: Aboriginal musicians, the didgeridoo and circular breathing
summary: No black players in Australian jazz; talk of the didgeridoo, circular breathing and a player Rowe heard imitating a truck meeting a kangaroo.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Okay. Is there an integrated jazz scene in Australia at all?
I mean like black and white players?

There aren’t any black players. The aboriginals, they’re there, but as far as I know there aren’t any — there’s been a few aboriginal tennis players, but they don’t seem to be into jazz. There’s quite a few country & western singers and guitar players, and there’s a guy that comes along where we play on a Friday night with the didgeridoo.
I was going to ask you when you might add that to your arsenal.
You can circular breathe and all that?

I can circular breathe already on the trumpet. It’s mind over matter, like learning to juggle three balls. Once you can do it it’s easy. But you just have to keep your lips, you have to keep air going while you close your throat and breathe through your nose. You have to get somebody to show you, really, and then you’ll know. But with the didgeridoo, the hole, it’s not just a little hole like in the trumpet, or a straw or something, the hole is that big. And you’re blowing a lot of air right through. And you have to breathe almost, it’s continuous. Plus you’ve got to buzz and make this sound, and they’re doing all these © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -11-
things with their throat. And they’re the most amazing sounds. Animal sounds and the sounds of the forests and birds and stuff, all from this pipe. Incredible.
Yeah. I heard a fellow from Australia do it. He was aborigine and he went on for five, ten minutes. I was just enthralled.
He played amazingly. And he had titles for the songs. Like one was about a truck going down a highway in Australia and the things that it met.
And as he did it, you could see, oh my God he’s doing the truck and it’s going to run over this animal here.
